input:
This case describes a defect-reduction project that was carried out on a filling line, in which the reject rate was cut from 5.5% to 2.4% over the course of one quarter, corresponding to a reduction of 3.1 percentage points. At 217k units per year, it is estimated that the change avoids about 6727 rejected units per year, which gives a helpful sense of the scale of the improvement in practical terms.

It is worth explaining the relationship between these figures. The reject rate expresses the proportion of production that the line rejects, and the number of rejected units that are avoided over a year is obtained by applying the reduction in that rate to the annual volume of production. The two figures therefore describe one and the same improvement in two different ways: the rate is the more useful figure for comparing the performance of this line with the performance of other lines, since it does not depend on how much a line produces, whereas the count of avoided units is the more useful figure for assessing the value of the improvement, although it will naturally change if the production volume changes.

One caveat should be attached to these results. The quarter in question included a planned shutdown, and the rates are not adjusted for it, which means that the comparison is drawn across a period that was not entirely representative of normal production. The figures should accordingly be read as the rates that were actually recorded, with the avoided count derived from them at the stated volume.
target:
A defect-reduction project on a filling line cut the reject rate from 5.5% to 2.4% over one quarter, a reduction of 3.1 percentage points. At 217k units per year, the change avoids about 6727 rejected units per year.

The reject rate is the share of production the line discards, so the avoided count follows from the rate reduction applied to the annual volume: the project changed the rate, and the count is that change expressed in units at the stated throughput. Both figures describe the same improvement on different scales. The rate states what the line now does with each unit it fills, independently of how many units pass through; the count states what the improvement is worth across a year of production at the current volume, and it would move with the volume even if the rate held steady. A reader comparing this line with another should compare rates, while a reader costing the improvement should work from the count and the volume it assumes.

The quarter included a planned shutdown, and the rates are not adjusted for it. Production during the quarter was therefore interrupted in a way the figures do not correct for, and the comparison between the rate before the project and the rate after it is a comparison across a quarter that was not a normal production period. The improvement is reported on that basis: the rates are the rates as recorded, the avoided count is derived from them at the stated annual volume, and neither figure has been restated to remove the shutdown.
